title: Rational polynomial models for finite-dimensional sl2 modules
statement:
Let $W$ be a finite-dimensional $\mathbf Q$-vector space, and let $E,F,H\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbf Q}(W)$ satisfy $HE-EH=2E$, $HF-FH=-2F$, and $EF-FE=H$. Assume $E$ and $F$ are nilpotent and $H$ is diagonalizable with integer eigenvalues. For each integer $n\geq0$, let $P_n\subset\mathbf Q[X,Y]$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] be the vector space with basis $X^{n-i}Y^i$ for $0\leq i\leq n$, equipped with the operators $e_n=X\partial/\partial Y$, $f_n=Y\partial/\partial X$, and $h_n=X\partial/\partial X-Y\partial/\partial Y$, where $\partial/\partial X,\partial/\partial Y$ are the formal partial derivatives [def-weil-pbc-polynomial-partial-derivative]. There are a finite set $I$, nonnegative integers $n_i$ for $i\in I$, and a $\mathbf Q$-linear isomorphism $T:W\xrightarrow{\sim}\bigoplus_{i\in I}P_{n_i}$ such that
$$TE=(\bigoplus_{i\in I}e_{n_i})T,\qquad TF=(\bigoplus_{i\in I}f_{n_i})T,\qquad TH=(\bigoplus_{i\in I}h_{n_i})T.$$
The empty direct sum is permitted and gives the assertion for $W=0$.

source.place: Theorem 23.70 and its proof, printed pp.507-508 (characteristic-zero integration and Weyl complete reducibility); Example 22.33, printed p.472 (homogeneous polynomial models). Agent-stated explicit rational Lie-module consequence, with the transpose substitution convention specified in the report, not an integral-lattice assertion.

proof.text: We use strong induction on $\dim_{\mathbf Q}W$ for all triples satisfying the stated hypotheses. If $W=0$, take $I=\varnothing$ and the unique linear isomorphism. Otherwise let $S\subset\mathbf Z$ be the finite nonempty set of eigenvalues of $H$, let $m=\max S$, and choose $0\ne v\in\ker(H-m)$. The relation $HE=EH+2E$ gives $H(Ev)=(m+2)Ev$; maximality of $m$ forces $Ev=0$. All these choices are over $\mathbf Q$, since diagonalizability with integer eigenvalues is an assumption.

source.place: Agent expansion of the characteristic-zero highest-weight calculation supporting Theorem 23.70 and Example 22.33.

proof.text: Put $u_j=F^jv$ for $j\ge0$. The identities $HF=FH-2F$ and $EF=FE+H$ give, by induction, $Hu_j=(m-2j)u_j$ and $Eu_{j+1}=(j+1)(m-j)u_j$. Explicitly the first induction starts at $Hv=mv$ and multiplies by $F$; the second starts at $EFv=Hv$ and its next coefficient is $j(m-j+1)+(m-2j)=(j+1)(m-j)$. Nilpotence of $F$ gives a largest $r\ge0$ with $u_r\ne0$, and $u_{r+1}=0$. The second identity at $j=r$ yields $(r+1)(m-r)u_r=0$. Over $\mathbf Q$ we conclude $m=r$. Write $n=r$, so $n\ge0$, $u_0,\ldots,u_n$ are nonzero, and $u_{n+1}=0$.

source.place: Agent calculation of the primitive-vector string; compare Example 22.33, p.472.

proof.text: The eigenvalues $n-2j$ for $0\le j\le n$ are pairwise distinct. Thus $u_0,\ldots,u_n$ are linearly independent: apply $\prod_{\ell\ne j}(H-(n-2\ell))/(2\ell-2j)$ to any linear relation to isolate its $u_j$ term. Let $U$ be their span. The preceding formulas show that $H$, $E$, and $F$ preserve $U$, including the endpoints $Eu_0=0$ and $Fu_n=0$. Hence these vectors are a basis of a nonzero invariant subspace $U\subseteq W$.

source.place: Agent expansion of the highest-weight string construction.

proof.text: For $b_j=X^{n-j}Y^j$, the monomial and derivative definitions give $e_nb_j=jb_{j-1}$, $f_nb_j=(n-j)b_{j+1}$, and $h_nb_j=(n-2j)b_j$, with the zero-coefficient endpoint terms interpreted as zero. Define $A:U\to P_n$ by $A(u_j)=c_jb_j$, where $c_j=n!/(n-j)!\in\mathbf Q^\times$. Distinct monomials are independent by the polynomial definition, so $A$ is a linear isomorphism. For $j\ge1$, $c_j=(n-j+1)c_{j-1}$ makes $AEu_j=j(n-j+1)c_{j-1}b_{j-1}=e_nAu_j$; for $j<n$, $c_{j+1}=(n-j)c_j$ gives $AFu_j=f_nAu_j$. The endpoint equalities and $AHu_j=h_nAu_j$ follow directly from the displayed formulas. This also covers $n=0$, with $c_0=1$.

source.place: Example 22.33, printed p.472; agent normalization for the differential operators of the item.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-sl2-invariant-complement] to the finite-dimensional rational space $W$ and the invariant subspace $U$ just constructed. Its three commutator hypotheses are exactly the hypotheses of the item. It supplies a common invariant complement $C$ with $W=U\oplus C$. The restrictions of $E,F$ to $C$ are nilpotent, and the commutator identities restrict to $C$. To check the remaining induction hypothesis, for $s\in S$ use the polynomial projector $p_s(H)=\prod_{t\in S,\,t\ne s}(H-t)/(s-t)$. It preserves $C$, and $\sum_s p_s(H)=1$ and $\operatorname{im}p_s(H)\subseteq\ker(H-s)$ follow by evaluating on an eigenbasis of $W$. Consequently $C=\bigoplus_{s\in S}(C\cap\ker(H-s))$. Thus $H|_C$ is diagonalizable with integer eigenvalues, and $\dim C<\dim W$ because $U\ne0$.

source.place: Theorem 23.70, proof (a), printed p.507, Weyl input; agent verification that restrictions satisfy the induction hypotheses.

proof.text: The induction hypothesis gives $B:C\xrightarrow{\sim}\bigoplus_{i\in J}P_{n_i}$ intertwining all three restricted operators. Let $I=\{*\}\sqcup J$, assign $n_*=n$, and set $T(u+c)=(A(u),B(c))$ under $W=U\oplus C$. Its inverse sends $(p,q)$ to $A^{-1}(p)+B^{-1}(q)$, so it is a rational linear isomorphism. Invariance of both summands and the three identities for $A$ and $B$ give the required three identities for $T$ on every $u+c$. This completes the dimension induction and produces a finite set $I$; the base case already includes its empty instance.

source.place: Agent assembly of the string model with Weyl complements; Example 22.33 and Theorem 23.70, p.507.
